facts.text: Brake dead time is the pause between the brake command and the first braking effect; brake build-up time is the further period until the brakes reach their full force.
facts.quote: Brake dead time is the pause between the brake command and the first braking effect, and build-up time is the further period until the brakes reach their full force.

facts.text: Most brakes on heavy machines are hydraulic, using oil under pressure, or pneumatic, using compressed air.
facts.quote: Most are hydraulic (oil under pressure) or pneumatic (compressed air).

facts.text: Brake dead time is also called brake-fill time or response time; braking does not begin until pressure is high enough for the brake pads to grip.
facts.quote: Until the pressure is high enough for the brake pads to grip, nothing happens: that is the dead time, also called brake-fill time or response time.

facts.text: Engineers model brake build-up as a ramp or a first-order lag, a curve that rises quickly at first and then flattens.
facts.quote: Engineers model the build-up as a ramp or as a "first-order lag", a curve that rises quickly at first and then flattens.

facts.text: A published 2026 figure for a tracked vehicle's electro-hydraulic brake gives pressure response under 0.3 s; the figure is specific to that architecture.
facts.quote: each specific to one architecture: pressure response under 0.3 s for a tracked vehicle's electro-hydraulic brake (2026)

facts.text: A published 2025 figure for a mining electric vehicle's brake-by-wire gives 0.41 s to reach the design value; the figure is architecture-specific.
facts.quote: 0.41 s to reach the design value for a mining electric vehicle's brake-by-wire (2025)

facts.text: A published 1989 figure gives about 0.5 s inherent delay for road-truck air brakes; the figure is architecture-specific on-road evidence.
facts.quote: about 0.5 s inherent delay for road-truck air brakes (1989)

facts.text: The US mining rule assumes system response time of 0.5 s for equipment up to 36,000 lb, rising in steps to 2.5 s above 400,000 lb, about 181 t.
facts.quote: the US mining rule's assumed system response time of 0.5 s for equipment up to 36,000 lb, rising in steps to 2.5 s above 400,000 lb (about 181 t).

facts.text: A historic US mining study reported 1 to 2 s of additional lag for retarders on large haul trucks.
facts.quote: A historic US mining study reported 1 to 2 s of additional lag for retarders on large haul trucks

facts.text: A road simulation round robin prescribed 0.2 s of actuator delay and 0.4 s of brake build-up.
facts.quote: a road simulation round robin prescribed 0.2 s of actuator delay and 0.4 s of build-up [Chapter 8].

facts.text: ISO 3450 measures stopping distance from brake-control actuation to standstill, including brake dead time and build-up but excluding operator reaction time.
facts.quote: ISO 3450 measures stopping distance from the moment the brake control is actuated to standstill, so it includes dead time and build-up but excludes the operator's reaction.

facts.text: South African guidance measures brake response time from brake application until deceleration reaches 10 percent of g, about 1 m/s².
facts.quote: South African guidance measures brake response time from brake application to the moment deceleration reaches 10 percent of g, about 1 m/s² [Chapter 8].

facts.text: A brake validation program should state which brake timing and stopping-distance measurement convention it uses.
facts.quote: A validation program should state which convention it uses.

facts.text: Brake dead time varies with oil temperature, accumulator charge and wear, and on the automated braking path also with the electronics between the collision system and brake valve.
facts.quote: It changes with oil temperature, with how much the accumulators (pressure reservoirs) are charged, with wear, and on the automatic path with the electronics between the collision system and the brake valve.

facts.text: Brake timing measurements must be performed for the automated brake path, not just the pedal path.
facts.quote: measurements "must be done for the automated brake path, not just the pedal path"

facts.text: Brake characterization tests should identify dead time, rise time, gain, saturation, hysteresis and release time.
facts.quote: tests should identify dead time, rise time, gain, saturation, hysteresis and release time

facts.text: The spread of brake delay matters as much as its average for brake characterization.
facts.quote: the spread of the delay matters as much as its average [Chapter 8].

facts.text: At work-site speeds, the delay contribution to stopping distance can equal or exceed the braking contribution.
facts.quote: At work-site speeds the delay term can equal or exceed the braking term

facts.text: An error of half a second in assumed brake dead time produces a stopping-distance error of about 2 m at 15 km/h.
facts.quote: an error of half a second in the assumed dead time is an error of about 2 m at 15 km/h.

facts.text: The booklet found no published brake delay distributions for production wheel loaders, articulated haulers or haul trucks across hydraulic, pneumatic, hydrostatic, wet-disc and blended brake systems.
facts.quote: The booklet found no published delay distributions for production wheel loaders, articulated haulers or haul trucks across hydraulic, pneumatic, hydrostatic, wet-disc and blended brake systems

facts.text: Brake delay distributions for production wheel loaders, articulated haulers and haul trucks must be measured rather than taken from published distributions.
facts.quote: "they must be measured".

facts.text: The booklet recommends a latency sweep with at least 10 repetitions across oil temperatures per machine family among the first physical tests after the prototype arrives.
facts.quote: It recommends a latency sweep with at least 10 repetitions across oil temperatures per machine family among the first physical tests after the prototype arrives [Chapter 8].
